content.text: Have you ever noticed how a straw in a glass of water appears to be bent or broken at the water surface? Or how a swimming pool looks shallower than it actually is? These everyday observations are caused by the refraction of light. Refraction is the change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in the wave's speed. It is one of the most important phenomena in optics and has countless applications, from corrective lenses and cameras to fibre optic telecommunications and medical endoscopes.

In this lesson, we will explore why light refracts, learn the mathematical law that governs refraction (Snell's law), investigate the fascinating phenomenon of total internal reflection, and see how these principles are applied in modern technology.

Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when it passes from one medium into another medium of different optical density. The change in direction occurs because the speed of light changes as it moves between media. Light travels fastest in a vacuum (approximately
m/s) and slower in denser media such as glass, water, or diamond.
When light passes from a less optically dense medium (like air) into a more optically dense medium (like glass):
The light bends towards the normal.
When light passes from a more optically dense medium into a less optically dense medium:
The light bends away from the normal.

The frequency of light does not change during refraction because the number of wave crests arriving at the boundary per second must equal the number leaving per second. Since the speed changes but the frequency does not, the wavelength must change (recall

To understand why light changes direction, consider wavefronts approaching a boundary at an angle. When the wavefront hits the boundary between air and glass, the part of the wavefront that enters the glass first slows down, while the rest of the wavefront is still travelling at the faster speed in air. This causes the wavefront to pivot, changing the direction of wave travel. This is similar to how a line of marching soldiers would change direction if one end of the line hit mud and slowed down before the other end.

If light hits the boundary along the normal (at 90 degrees to the surface), all parts of the wavefront hit the boundary at the same time. In this case, the light slows down but does not change direction. Refraction only causes a change in direction when the light enters the new medium at an angle to the normal.

Total internal reflection (TIR) is a phenomenon that occurs when light travelling in an optically denser medium hits the boundary with a less dense medium at a sufficiently large angle of incidence. Instead of refracting and passing into the less dense medium, the light is completely reflected back into the denser medium.

Diamond has a very small critical angle, which means that light is easily trapped inside a diamond by total internal reflection. This is why diamonds sparkle so brilliantly when cut with many facets.

When a ray of light passes through a rectangular glass block, it refracts twice: once when entering the block and once when leaving. On entering, the light bends towards the normal (because it is going from air into glass, a denser medium). On leaving, it bends away from the normal (because it is going from glass back into air, a less dense medium). Because the two surfaces are parallel, the ray that emerges from the block is parallel to the original incident ray but displaced sideways. This lateral displacement increases with the thickness of the block and the angle of incidence.

A prism is a block of glass (or other transparent material) with flat, polished surfaces that are not parallel to each other. When light enters a prism, it refracts at the first surface (bending towards the normal) and refracts again at the second surface (bending away from the normal). Because the surfaces are not parallel, the two refractions do not cancel out, and the light emerges at an angle to its original direction. The overall change in direction is called the angle of deviation.

Prisms are important because different colours (wavelengths) of light have slightly different refractive indices in glass, causing them to refract by different amounts. This separates white light into its component colours, a phenomenon called dispersion, which we will study in detail in a later lesson.
Applications of Refraction and Total Internal Reflection

Optical fibres are thin, flexible strands of high-purity glass or plastic that transmit light over long distances using total internal reflection. Light enters one end of the fibre and bounces along the inside, reflecting off the walls at angles greater than the critical angle. Because the light is totally internally reflected, very little energy is lost, allowing signals to travel many kilometres.

Optical fibres consist of a core (a thin glass strand with a high refractive index) surrounded by a cladding (a layer of glass with a slightly lower refractive index). The difference in refractive index between the core and cladding ensures that total internal reflection occurs at the core-cladding boundary.

Optical fibres are the backbone of modern telecommunications. They can carry vastly more data than traditional copper cables, are immune to electromagnetic interference, and are lighter and thinner. The internet, telephone networks, and cable television all rely heavily on optical fibre technology.

Medical endoscopes use bundles of optical fibres to look inside the human body without surgery. One bundle carries light into the body to illuminate the area being examined, and another bundle carries the reflected light back to the doctor's eye or a camera. This allows doctors to examine the digestive system, lungs, joints, and other internal structures.

Prisms using total internal reflection are used in binoculars, periscopes, and some camera systems. A right-angled glass prism can reflect light through 90 degrees or 180 degrees by total internal reflection, producing clearer images than a metal mirror because no energy is lost by absorption.

Misconception 1: Light always bends when it enters a new medium

Light only changes direction if it hits the boundary at an angle to the normal. If light hits the boundary along the normal (perpendicular to the surface), it slows down (or speeds up) but continues in the same straight-line direction. Refraction is a change in speed that only produces a change in direction when the wave arrives at an angle.
Misconception 2: The frequency of light changes during refraction

The frequency of a wave does not change when it moves from one medium to another. The speed and wavelength change, but the frequency remains constant. If the frequency changed, wave crests would be created or destroyed at the boundary, which does not happen.
Misconception 3: Total internal reflection can happen when going from a less dense to a more dense medium

Total internal reflection can only occur when light is travelling from a more optically dense medium (higher refractive index) towards a less optically dense medium (lower refractive index). When light goes from air into glass, total internal reflection cannot occur; the light will always partially refract into the glass.
Misconception 4: Optical density is the same as physical density

Optical density is related to how much a material slows down light, while physical density is mass per unit volume. Although they often correlate, they are not identical. For example, some oils have lower physical density than water but higher refractive indices.
Misconception 5: The critical angle is the angle at which refraction begins

The critical angle is actually the angle of incidence above which total internal reflection occurs. Below the critical angle, light partially refracts and partially reflects. At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the boundary. Above the critical angle, all light is reflected back into the denser medium.
